[start-outcomes] After this part you should be able to
1. Derive the steady 2D heat-conduction PDE from an energy balance and Fourier’s law, and write it as {∂}[E]{∂}ᵀT = −q_h .
2. Classify boundary conditions as Dirichlet (essential) or Neumann (natural) and write them for a rectangular domain.
3. Derive the bilinear shape functions N_1 …N_4 of the four-node element and use them to interpolate T(x, y).
4. Differentiate the approximation to obtain the temperature gradient and the heat flux at any point of an element.

[notes-n1] Notes 1. Why a 2D field problem, and what FEM delivers
Everything in the first half of the course was one-dimensional: a bar, a beam, a truss, a frame. The unknowns sat on a line. From here on the unknown is a field : a temperature T(x, y) defined at every point of a plate. We cannot solve for infinitely many values, so we solve for a finite number of them at nodes and let the element interpolate in between. That is the whole idea of the method.
FEM is “nothing”, and FEM is “everything” Nothing: FEM adds no new physics. It is only a way to turn a differential equation into simultaneous algebraic equations in matrix form. Everything: the same machinery solves heat, seepage, stress, vibration and fluid flow. Learn it once, on the simplest field problem, and reuse it.
## Scalar field first, vector field later
Heat conduction is a scalar field problem: one unknown per node, the temperature T̂_i. Plane stress, later in the course, is a vector field problem: two unknowns per node, the displacements u_i and v_i. Every idea of this part — shape functions, boundary conditions, assembly — appears in both; plane stress only has bigger matrices.
[Figure: Left: a scalar field, one number at each node. Right: a vector field, two numbers at each node.]
## Where civil engineers meet conduction
- Mass concrete. Heat of hydration in dams, rafts and pile caps: the temperature rise and the gradient between core and surface drive early-age cracking.
- Fire engineering. Temperature rise in steel sections and tunnel linings decides when strength is lost; the input is a 2D conduction model of the section.
- Pavements and decks. Daily thermal gradients through a bridge deck or a pavement slab produce stresses that design codes make us check.
- Ground and geothermal. Ground freezing, energy piles and buried pipelines are conduction problems in soil — and seepage uses the same equation.
[Figure: A heated plate under a channel flow. The solid plate obeys this part’s conduction PDE; at its interface with the fluid it receives a temperature and returns a heat flux — one Dirichlet and one Neumann condition (§3). Image: preCICE tutorials, “Flow over a heated plate”, LGPL-3.0, github.com/precice/tutorials.]
Key points:
- The unknown is a field T(x, y); FEM solves for nodal values and interpolates between them.
- FEM adds no physics; it turns a PDE into [K]{T̂} = {r}.
- Scalar field: one unknown per node. Plane stress will have two.
Quick check (not graded): What does the finite element method add to the physics of heat conduction?
Options: Fourier’s law | Nothing — it only discretises the PDE | A heat-generation term
Explanation shown after answering: Nothing. The physics is the energy balance and Fourier’s law; FEM is a numerical method that turns the resulting PDE into algebraic equations.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. From the energy balance to the PDE
Take a small rectangle dx by dy inside the plate, of unit thickness. The dependent variables are the heat fluxes q_x and q_y (W m^{−2}): energy per unit time per unit area crossing a face. Heat enters through the near faces and leaves through the far faces.
[Figure: The differential element: fluxes in and out, generation q_h inside (text Fig. 2.1).]
The flux on the far face is the near-face flux plus its change across the element, a first-order Taylor expansion. The net inflow in the x-direction is therefore
EQUATION (2.2): [equation e_Qx: source not available in the page]
and by the same argument in the y-direction
EQUATION (2.3): [equation e_Qy: source not available in the page]
Inside, heat is generated at a rate q_h per unit volume (W m^{−3}), for example the hydration of cement, and the element stores energy as its temperature rises:
EQUATION (2.5): [equation e_Qh: source not available in the page]
## Conservation of energy
Rate of change of stored energy = net conduction in + heat generated. Every term carries the factor dx dy, the volume of the element per unit thickness, so it cancels:
EQUATION (2.6): [equation e_balance: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_balance2: source not available in the page]
Per unit thickness Every quantity is multiplied by the same thickness t, which cancels, so we take t = 1. Nothing changes for a plate of any thickness as long as the faces are insulated.
## Fourier’s law closes the system
The balance has three unknowns (T, q_x, q_y) and one equation. Fourier’s law supplies the other two: heat flows down the temperature gradient, in proportion to the conductivity k (W m^{−1} K^{−1}). The minus sign is the physics: flux points from hot to cold.
EQUATION (2.7): [equation e_fourier: source not available in the page]
[Figure: Flux points down the gradient: from the hot side to the cold side.]
Substituting (2.7) into the balance gives one equation in T alone:
EQUATION (2.10): [equation e_pde_t: source not available in the page]
## Steady state: the PDE we discretise
Drop the time derivative. This is the equation you must be able to write from memory: the divergence of the flux equals the source.
EQUATION (2.11): [equation e_pde: source not available in the page]
Two special cases you have met before: with constant isotropic k it is Poisson’s equation, and with no source it is Laplace’s equation — the same equation as potential flow in fluid mechanics and seepage in soil mechanics.
EQUATION : [equation e_poisson: source not available in the page]
Unit check Each term of (2.11) is W m^{−3}: (W m^{−1} K^{−1})(K m^{−2}). The source q_h sits on the right with a minus sign because we moved it across; a positive source makes the field concave, a hill.
## The matrix form we will reuse
Write the operator as a row of derivatives, a material matrix and a column of derivatives. This is the slide that pays off in plane stress, where the same pattern appears with a 3 × 3 [E] and a 2 × 3 operator.
EQUATION (2.12): [equation e_matrix: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (2.13): [equation e_compact: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (2.14): [equation e_defs: source not available in the page]
Order matters {∂} is a row of operators, not numbers: it acts on whatever stands to its right. You cannot commute it past a function.
## Worked step · the y-direction balance (Activity 2)
In through y = 0: q_y dx. Out through y = dy: (q_y + ∂q_y/∂y dy) dx. Net inflow Q_y = −∂q_y/∂y dx dy, equation (2.3). Add Q_x, Q_y and Q_h, set the sum equal to the stored-energy rate Q_E, cancel dx dy, and (2.6) follows.
Key points:
- Energy balance on dx × dy, then Fourier’s law, gives (2.11): divergence of flux = source.
- Every term of (2.11) is W m^{−3}.
- Matrix form {∂}[E]{∂}ᵀT = −q_h; [E] = diag(k_x, k_y).
Quick check (not graded): What are the units of the heat-generation term q_h in (2.11)?
Options: W m^{−2} | W m^{−3} | W m^{−1} K^{−1}
Explanation shown after answering: q_h is heat generated per unit volume, W m^{−3}, the same as k ∂²T/∂x². A flux (W m^{−2}) is per unit area; conductivity is W m^{−1} K^{−1}.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. Boundary conditions: essential and natural
A PDE alone is not a problem. On every part of the boundary we must specify either the temperature or the flux. There are only two kinds of condition, and the whole of the finite element treatment depends on telling them apart.
EQUATION (2.16): [equation e_dirichlet: source not available in the page]
Dirichlet, or essential The temperature T̄ is known on the edge. FEM must impose it on the unknowns: the corresponding rows and columns of the assembled system are modified.
Neumann, or natural The boundary flux q_b is known, positive inward, and enters through the outward unit normal n = (n_x, n_y). FEM does not impose it: it appears by itself as a load, from the integration by parts in Part 2.
[Figure: The outward unit normal on each edge of a rectangular domain.]
## Rectangular domains
On a rectangle the normal is one of (±1, 0) or (0, ±1), so (2.15) loses one term on every edge:
EQUATION : [equation e_rect_v: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_rect_h: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_insul: source not available in the page]
## What FEM does with each kind
Condition What is known Where it enters the FEM Action in Part 2
Dirichlet · essential T̄ on the edge imposed on the assembled system by modifying rows and columns of [K] row–column elimination
Neumann · natural q_b on the edge appears in the boundary vector {b} produced by integration by parts {b} = ∫{N}ᵀq_n ds
Insulated · natural, q_b = 0 no flux contributes nothing: the boundary integral is zero do nothing
The most common error Trying to “impose” an insulated edge. It needs no action at all. The names come from the integration by parts: the natural condition is the term that falls out of it; the essential one must be enforced on the unknowns.
## Worked example · label the plate (Activity 3, text Exercise 2.5)
[Figure: Plate 0.15 m × 0.05 m, k = 450 W m^{−1} K^{−1}, q_h = 1 × 10^7 W m^{−3}, unit thickness.]
Edge Type Equation FEM action
top Dirichlet T = 300 K impose on the system
left Dirichlet T = 400 K impose on the system
right Neumann n = (1, 0): k ∂T/∂x = q_b = +1 × 10^6 W m^{−2} load in {b}
bottom Neumann, q_b = 0 ∂T/∂y = 0 nothing
Well-posed: every edge has a condition and T is fixed on two edges, so the temperature level is pinned. The inward flux on the right edge is positive q_b; the flux-vector component q_x there points along −n and is negative, q_x = −10^6 W m^{−2}.
Key points:
- Dirichlet = essential = imposed. Neumann = natural = appears from the integration by parts. Insulated = do nothing.
- q_b is positive inward; on a rectangle only one derivative survives per edge.
- A problem is well-posed when every edge has a condition and T is pinned somewhere.
Quick check (not graded): An edge of the plate is insulated. In the finite element model, what must you do about it?
Options: Impose ∂T/∂y = 0 on the nodes of that edge | Nothing: its boundary integral is zero | Set T = 0 on those nodes
Explanation shown after answering: An insulated edge is a natural condition with q_b = 0, so the boundary term {b} it would produce is zero. No action is needed.

[notes-n4] Notes 4. The four-node element and its shape functions
The four-node rectangular element has one degree of freedom at each corner, the temperature T̂_i, numbered anticlockwise from the bottom-left corner. We need a rule for T at any point inside the element in terms of these four numbers. The rule is a polynomial with four coefficients.
[Figure: The element a × b, nodes 1 to 4 anticlockwise from the origin (text Fig. 2.2).]
## Step 1 · assume a polynomial (2.17)
EQUATION (2.17): [equation e_poly: source not available in the page]
Four unknowns need four coefficients. The xy term, rather than x² or y², keeps the function linear along every edge, which is what makes neighbouring elements agree.
## Step 2 · evaluate at the nodes (2.18)
EQUATION (2.18): [equation e_nodes: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_nodes_matrix: source not available in the page]
## Step 3 · solve for the coefficients (2.19)
EQUATION (2.19): [equation e_coeffs: source not available in the page]
Check: if all four nodal values are equal to T_0, then a_1 = T_0 and a_2 = a_3 = a_4 = 0, so T = T_0 everywhere. A uniform field is reproduced exactly.
## Step 4 · collect by nodal value (2.20)–(2.22)
EQUATION (2.20): [equation e_collect: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (2.21): [equation e_shape: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (2.22): [equation e_T_N: source not available in the page]
Each nodal value is multiplied by its own function of position: its shape function N_i(x, y). The row {N} and the column {T̂}ᵀ are the two objects the rest of the course is built from.
## What a shape function looks like
[Figure: N_3 as a surface (left) and N_1…N_4 as colour maps (right): each is 1 at its own node, 0 at the other three, and curved inside because of the xy term.]
[Figure: The same four functions inside commercial code. Image: PyMAPDL documentation, “Build a finite element model”, © ANSYS, Inc., MIT licence.]
## Three properties you can check in 30 seconds
EQUATION : [equation e_kron: source not available in the page]
Kronecker delta. So T at node j equals T̂_j: the nodal unknowns really are nodal temperatures. Check N_2 at node 3: N_2(a, b) = a(b − b)/(ab) = 0.
EQUATION : [equation e_pou: source not available in the page]
Partition of unity. A uniform temperature is reproduced exactly, the test we did on the coefficients.
EQUATION : [equation e_edge: source not available in the page]
Linear along each edge. On y = 0 only nodes 1 and 2 matter, and T varies linearly between them. The neighbouring element shares those two nodes and the same straight line, so T is continuous across element boundaries (C^0).
## From one element to the mesh
[Figure: One nodal value lifts one tent. In 1D the basis function of node i is a hat over the two elements that share it; in 2D it is a tent over every element around the node. That is why node i couples only to its neighbours and the global matrix is sparse (Part 2). Images: Langtangen and Mardal, Introduction to Numerical Methods for Variational Problems (Springer, 2019), github.com/hplgit/fem-book, MIT licence.]
## Worked example · evaluate and interpolate (Activity 4)
a = 2 m, b = 1 m, point (x, y) = (1.5, 0.3) m, nodal temperatures T̂ = {100, 140, 160, 120} K.
[Figure: The point (1.5, 0.3) in the 2 m × 1 m element.]
EQUATION : [equation e_act4_N: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_act4_sum: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_act4_T: source not available in the page]
Node 2 carries half the weight because the point is nearest to it. The sum of the four weights is 1, as it must be.
Key points:
- T = {N}{T̂}ᵀ with the bilinear N_i of (2.21).
- Kronecker delta, partition of unity, linear edges: three checks that catch most errors.
- At (1.5, 0.3): N = 0.175, 0.525, 0.225, 0.075 and T = 136.0 K.
Quick check (not graded): At the centre of the element (a/2, b/2), what is the value of each shape function?
Options: 1 | 1/2 | 1/4
Explanation shown after answering: N_i(a/2, b/2) = (a/2)(b/2)/(ab) = 1/4 for every i, and the four values sum to 1.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. Gradient and flux inside an element
Differentiate the approximation T = {N}{T̂}ᵀ and the derivatives land on the shape functions, because the nodal values are constants. The gradient at any point is a 2 × 4 matrix of shape-function derivatives times the nodal vector:
EQUATION (2.33): [equation e_grad: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_dN: source not available in the page]
Read the matrix: ∂N_i/∂x depends on y only and ∂N_i/∂y on x only. Across an element edge the gradient, and therefore the flux, generally jumps — the approximation is continuous but its derivative is not.
## From gradient to flux
EQUATION : [equation e_flux_vec: source not available in the page]
Fourier’s law in matrix form: flux = −[E] × gradient. The same 2 × 4 matrix {∂}ᵀ{N} will be used twice: for the flux now, and for the conductance matrix in Part 2:
EQUATION : [equation e_k_preview: source not available in the page]
## Worked example · gradient and flux at (1.5, 0.3) (Activity 5)
Same element and data as Activity 4, with k_x = k_y = 2 W m^{−1} K^{−1}.
EQUATION : [equation e_act5_dN: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_act5_grad: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_act5_q: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_act5_qy: source not available in the page]
Both components of the flux are negative: heat flows towards decreasing x and y, away from the hottest node 3 at (a, b).
## The eight-node element in one paragraph
[Figure: Four corner nodes and four mid-side nodes (text Fig. 2.3).]
Add a node at the middle of each edge and the polynomial gains four terms, (2.31). The shape functions are quadratic along each edge, so they follow a curved temperature profile with fewer elements. The procedure is identical: evaluate at the eight nodes, invert, collect by nodal value. A corner function now dips below zero between its two mid-side neighbours, and the eight functions still sum to one.
EQUATION (2.31): [equation e_poly8: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation e_N8: source not available in the page]
Key points:
- Gradient = {∂}ᵀ{N}{T̂}ᵀ, a 2 × 4 matrix times the nodal vector; flux = −[E] × gradient.
- At (1.5, 0.3) with k = 2: ∂T/∂x = ∂T/∂y = 20 K m^{−1}, q_x = q_y = −40 W m^{−2}.
- The eight-node element is the same procedure with quadratic edges.
Quick check (not graded): At a point the temperature increases in the +x direction. The flux component q_x there is
Options: positive | negative | zero
Explanation shown after answering: q_x = −k ∂T/∂x. A positive gradient gives a negative flux: heat flows from hot to cold, towards −x.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. The pipeline: seven steps from PDE to answer
The method is a pipeline of seven steps. This part covered the first two; Part 2 does the other five on the text’s worked example and runs the MATLAB script.
- Governing PDE and boundary conditions · this part
- Element and shape functions · this part
- Galerkin weighted residual
- Integration by parts
- Element matrices [k], {q}, {b}
- Assembly, then impose T̄
- Solve and post-process
## Part 2’s worked example (text §2.3)
[Figure: A 1 m square plate with heat generation, two cold edges and two insulated edges, meshed with four elements.]
Square plate 1 m × 1 m, q_h = 600 W m^{−3}, k_x = k_y = 300 W m^{−1} K^{−1}; top and left edges at 0 °C, right and bottom edges insulated. Four 4-node elements by hand, then 64 elements in MATLAB, then software.
Before Part 2 Classify its four edges as in §3 and predict where the hottest point is. Write the prediction down; Part 2 checks it.
## The MATLAB skeleton follows the pipeline
% Local conductance matrix (text §2.3.1)
a = L/Nx; b = H/Ny;
s1 = b*kx/(3*a) + a*ky/(3*b);
s2 = -b*kx/(3*a) + a*ky/(6*b);
s3 = -b*kx/(6*a) - a*ky/(6*b);
s4 = b*kx/(6*a) - a*ky/(3*b);
k = [s1 s2 s3 s4; s2 s1 s4 s3; s3 s4 s1 s2; s4 s3 s2 s1];
fQ = a*b*Q/4*[1; 1; 1; 1]; % heat generation
% Assembly by connectivity, element 1 = nodes [1 2 5 4]
e1 = [1 2 5 4]; K(e1,e1) = K(e1,e1) + k; F(e1) = F(e1) + fQ;
% Essential conditions: rows and columns of known nodes removed
free = setdiff(1:n, fixed); T = zeros(n,1); T(fixed) = Tbar;
T(free) = K(free,free) \ (F(free) - K(free,fixed)*T(fixed));
- Lines 2–8: step 5, the element matrix and load from closed-form integrals (s_1…s_4 are derived in Part 2).
- Line 10: step 6, assembly — the connectivity list [1 2 5 4] is the element’s global node numbers.
- Lines 12–13: step 6, essential conditions by removing the rows and columns of the known nodes; step 7, solve with the backslash operator.
## To prepare
- Read text §2.2.2 and §2.3 (the worked example), about 12 pages.
- Redo Activities 4 and 5 for the point (0.5, 0.8) m — or use the exercises tab, which gives you new numbers each time.
- Classify the edges of the §2.3 plate and predict the hottest point.
- Bring MATLAB to the next session.
Key points:
- Seven steps: PDE + BCs, element, Galerkin, integration by parts, element matrices, assembly + impose, solve.
- Part 2: steps 3–7 on the 1 m plate, by hand with four elements and in MATLAB with 64.
Quick check (not graded): For the §2.3 plate (cold top and left edges, insulated right and bottom edges, uniform heat generation), where is the hottest point?
Options: The centre of the plate | The bottom-right corner | The top-left corner
Explanation shown after answering: Heat can only leave through the two cold edges. The point farthest from both, where the two insulated edges meet, is the bottom-right corner.

[examples-x3] Example 3 · Explain-type questions: model answers
Exam type explain, three sentences each: claim, reason, consequence Source FEM by Hand, §8.4 4 × 3 = 12 marks Questions Answer each in two or three sentences. State the claim, give the reason, and say what follows from it.
## Step 1 Why is nothing done at an insulated edge? [3]
An insulated edge is a natural condition with q_n = 0, so its boundary term t∫{N}q_n ds is zero. The Galerkin formulation satisfies it approximately without any action. A non-zero flux would instead enter {r} at the nodes of that edge.
## Step 2 What is the difference between an essential and a natural boundary condition, and how is each imposed? [3]
An essential condition prescribes the primary variable, the temperature T = T̄; a natural condition prescribes the secondary variable, the flux q_n. The essential condition is imposed on the assembled equations by striking the rows and columns of the known nodes, and the struck rows later give the heat flows there. The natural condition is never imposed: it appears by itself as a load through the boundary term of the integration by parts.
## Step 3 Why does every row of [k] add up to zero, and how is that used? [3]
Since ΣN_i = 1, a uniform temperature makes every gradient zero and conducts no heat, so [k]{1, 1, …}ᵀ = {0}. Consequently [k], and an unrestrained [K], are singular, which is why at least one temperature must be prescribed. Every row of a computed matrix can be checked in a few seconds by adding it up.
EQUATION : [equation x3_rowsum: source not available in the page]
## Step 4 How do the three-node and the four-node elements differ? [3]
The T3 field is a plane, so its gradient and flux are constant in each element. The Q4 field contains xy, so ∂T/∂x varies with y and ∂T/∂y with x. Both fields vary linearly along every side, so the temperature is continuous between elements while the flux jumps; on the same nodes the Q4 is usually more accurate, but in this course it is limited to rectangles, whereas triangles fit any shape.
Interpretation The examiner looks for the three parts in order. “Insulated means do nothing” alone is a claim without a reason and earns one mark of three; naming the boundary term and its value earns the other two. Marking scheme (suggested) · 12 What earns the marks Marks

SEAA 4243 Finite Element Method - shape functions of the rectangular elements
==============================================================================
Companion code for the Shape Function Explorer (2D Heat Transfer, Part 1).
What it does
Evaluates the shape functions N_i of the 4-node (Q4) and 8-node (Q8)
rectangular elements at a point, checks them, interpolates a nodal field,
and computes the gradient and the heat flux at that point.
Notation (text: Mohd Yassin et al., MSNM 2020, Sec. 2.2)
Element a x b. Local nodes 1-4 anticlockwise from the bottom-left corner;
the Q8 adds mid-side nodes 5-8 on the bottom,

[glossary-field-problem] Glossary: field problem
field problem: An unknown defined at every point of a region, such as T(x, y), rather than at a few discrete locations.

[glossary-scalar-field-vector-field] Glossary: scalar field · vector field
scalar field · vector field: One number per point (temperature) versus two or more per point (displacement u, v).

[glossary-heat-flux-q] Glossary: heat flux q
heat flux q: Energy crossing a unit area per unit time, W m^{−2} ; a vector with components q_x , q_y .

[glossary-fourier-s-law] Glossary: Fourier’s law
Fourier’s law: q = −k ∇T: flux is proportional to the temperature gradient and points from hot to cold.

[glossary-conductivity-k] Glossary: conductivity k
conductivity k: Material property, W m^{−1} K^{−1} ; [E] = diag(k_x , k_y ) for an orthotropic material.

[glossary-heat-generation-q-h] Glossary: heat generation q_h
heat generation q_h: Heat produced per unit volume, W m^{−3} , for example by cement hydration.

[glossary-steady-state] Glossary: steady state
steady state: Nothing changes with time: ∂T/∂t = 0, so the stored-energy term disappears.

[glossary-poisson-laplace] Glossary: Poisson · Laplace
Poisson · Laplace: Special cases of (2.11): constant isotropic k gives Poisson’s equation; no source gives Laplace’s equation.

[glossary-boundary-condition] Glossary: boundary condition
boundary condition: What is specified on the edge of the domain: the temperature or the flux. Needed on every part of the boundary.

[glossary-dirichlet-essential] Glossary: Dirichlet · essential
Dirichlet · essential: A known value of the unknown field on the edge, T = T̄. Imposed on the assembled equations.

[glossary-neumann-natural] Glossary: Neumann · natural
Neumann · natural: A known flux on the edge, q_b , positive inward. Appears by itself through the integration by parts.

[glossary-outward-normal-n] Glossary: outward normal n
outward normal n: Unit vector pointing out of the domain at an edge; on a rectangle (±1, 0) or (0, ±1).

[glossary-insulated-edge] Glossary: insulated edge
insulated edge: A natural condition with q_b = 0. Requires no action in the finite element model.

[glossary-well-posed] Glossary: well-posed
well-posed: Every edge has a condition and the temperature level is fixed somewhere, so the solution is unique.

[glossary-element-node] Glossary: element · node
element · node: A small region (here a rectangle a × b) and the points on it where the unknowns live.

[glossary-degree-of-freedom] Glossary: degree of freedom
degree of freedom: One unknown of the discrete system; one temperature per node for conduction.

[glossary-shape-function-n-i] Glossary: shape function N_i
shape function N_i: The function of position that multiplies nodal value i in the interpolation T = Σ N_i T̂_i .

[glossary-bilinear] Glossary: bilinear
bilinear: Linear in x and in y separately, with an xy term: the four-node element’s polynomial (2.17).

[glossary-kronecker-delta] Glossary: Kronecker delta
Kronecker delta: N_i = 1 at its own node and 0 at the others; so the nodal unknowns are nodal temperatures.

[glossary-partition-of-unity] Glossary: partition of unity
partition of unity: Σ N_i = 1 at every point; a uniform field is reproduced exactly.

[glossary-c-0-continuity] Glossary: C^0 continuity
C^0 continuity: T is continuous across element edges but its derivative generally jumps.

[glossary-gradient-matrix-n] Glossary: gradient matrix {∂}ᵀ{N}
gradient matrix {∂}ᵀ{N}: The 2 × 4 matrix of shape-function derivatives; gradient = {∂}ᵀ{N}{T̂}ᵀ.

[glossary-conductance-matrix-k] Glossary: conductance matrix [k]
conductance matrix [k]: The element matrix of Part 2, [k] = ∫∫{N}ᵀ{∂}[E]{∂}ᵀ{N} dy dx; the heat analogue of stiffness.

[glossary-assembly-connectivity] Glossary: assembly · connectivity
assembly · connectivity: Adding element matrices into the global system using each element’s list of global node numbers.
